items.title: 61428_Red Callender oral history interview
items.q: I remember one morning Blanton and I went by, and he played with Fletcher for hours. I just sat and marvelled.

ctx.x: Well, when you play the bass, it's very physical. All music is physical, but playing saxophone your fingers work and your body doesn't necessarily perspire. But when you play the bass with a big band, you maybe have to change shirts or undershirts a couple of times a night. So this is how Blanton first contracted TB, just improper care, you know. You know, he'd work in Chicago or somewhere like that, you're wringing wet, and you go hang out with somebody like Ben all night, and then you get wiped out. Blanton was…

Anyhow, he and I and Lee Young and Sweepea, or Billy Strayhorn, used to hang out a lot together. And I remember once Fletcher Henderson lived out here, too, over on Hoover Avenue on the East Side. I remember one morning Blanton and I went by, and he played with Fletcher for hours. I just sat and marvelled. There was no such thing as tape recorders then, and wire recorders were big, bulky things, so you couldn't take them around. So that's why I say some of the best music has never been recorded.
